questions.q: State the exact expression for the magnetic field at the centre of a circular loop of radius \( R \) carrying a steady current \( I \). Include the SI unit of each quantity.
questions.a: \( B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2R} \) with \( \mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7} \, \text{T·m/A} \), \( I \) in amperes (A), \( R \) in metres (m), giving \( B \) in tesla (T). A wrong answer like \( B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi R} \) reveals confusion with the straight‑wire formula; omitting \( \mu_0 \) or using gauss instead of tesla shows unit unawareness.

questions.q: Explain why the perpendicular components of the magnetic field cancel out when integrating over the entire circular loop for an axial point, while the axial components add up.
questions.a: For every current element \( d\vec{l} \) there is a diametrically opposite element \( d\vec{l}' \) whose perpendicular component \( dB_\perp \) is equal in magnitude but opposite in direction (radially outward vs inward), so they cancel pairwise. The axial components \( dB_x \) are both directed along the axis (same sense) and therefore add constructively. A student who says “perpendicular components cancel because the loop is symmetric” without mentioning pairwise opposition shows incomplete understanding of vector addition.

questions.q: A circular coil of 50 turns and radius 5.0 cm carries a current of 0.80 A. Calculate the magnetic field at a point on the axis 12 cm from the centre of the coil. Give your answer in tesla.

Two identical circular loops of radius \( R \) carry the same current \( I \). Loop A is a single turn; Loop B has 10 closely wound turns. Compare the magnetic field at the centre of each loop and at a point on the axis at distance \( x = R \) from the centre. Explain any differences in the ratio of fields.
questions.a: At the centre: \( B_A = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2R} \), \( B_B = \frac{\mu_0 (10I)}{2R} = 10 B_A \). At \( x = R \): \( B_A = \frac{\mu_0 I R^2}{2(2R^2)^{3/2}} = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2R} \cdot \frac{1}{2^{3/2}} \), \( B_B = 10 B_A \). The ratio \( B_B/B_A = 10 \) at both positions because the \( N \) factor multiplies the entire expression uniformly. A student who claims the ratio changes with \( x \) misunderstands that \( N \) is a simple multiplicative factor for closely wound turns of same radius.

questions.q: A student derives the axial field of a circular loop and writes \( B = \frac{\mu_0 I R}{2(x^2+R^2)^{3/2}} \). Identify the error and explain why it is dimensionally incorrect.
questions.a: The error is \( R \) instead of \( R^2 \) in the numerator. Dimensionally: \( \mu_0 I \) has units \( \text{T·m} \). The denominator \( (x^2+R^2)^{3/2} \) has units \( \text{m}^3 \). So \( \frac{\mu_0 I R}{...} \) gives \( \frac{\text{T·m} \cdot \text{m}}{\text{m}^3} = \text{T/m} \), not tesla. The correct \( R^2 \) gives \( \frac{\text{T·m} \cdot \text{m}^2}{\text{m}^3} = \text{T} \). A student missing this reveals poor dimensional analysis habit.

questions.q: Design a simple experiment using a battery, a variable resistor, a circular loop of wire, and a compass to verify that the magnetic field at the centre of the loop is directly proportional to the current. Describe the procedure, measurements, and how you would plot the data.
questions.a: Procedure: (1) Make a circular loop of known radius \( R \) (e.g., 10 cm) with insulated copper wire. (2) Connect it in series with a battery, a variable resistor (rheostat), and an ammeter. (3) Place a compass at the centre of the loop, aligning the loop’s plane with the magnetic meridian (so Earth’s field is along the axis). (4) Vary the rheostat to get different currents \( I \); for each, note the compass deflection \( \theta \) from the meridian. (5) The loop’s field \( B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2R} \) is perpendicular to Earth’s horizontal field \( B_H \); \( \tan\theta = B/B_H \). Plot \( \tan\theta \) vs \( I \); a straight line through origin confirms proportionality. A poor answer would omit the need to align the loop with the magnetic meridian or forget to use \( \tan\theta \).

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Observe a school laboratory ______: a circular copper loop connected to a battery and a compass needle placed at its centre.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can (1) derive the axial magnetic field formula from the Biot–Savart law by correctly resolving components and integrating over the loop, (2) compute the field at the centre and at any axial point for single or multi-turn loops with correct SI units, and (3) determine the field direction using the right‑hand thumb rule for a.
